variants.name: Pagy keyset paginator
variants.implementation_notes: Pagy's keyset paginator is the Rails realization: @pagy, @records = pagy(:keyset, Product.order(my_order).all) computes the page with a keyset algorithm (no OFFSET) while keeping Pagy's helper and URL machinery, and the pagy object carries the cursor strings for the next and previous links, so controllers get offset-free pagination without hand-writing the seek predicate. The hand-rolled WHERE (created_at, id) < (...) plus a base64 cursor remains the option outside a Rails view or when the token must be fully opaque to the client.
pitfalls: The keyset ordering must be deterministic and indexed: ordering by a mutable column such as updated_at lets rows move across the cursor between pages, so they appear twice or never.

A default_scope or a relation already materialized/limited before pagy(:keyset, ...) silently changes the sequence the cursor is computed from; keep the relation unpaginated and un-limited until Pagy sees it.

variants.name: Relay-style GraphQL connection (graphql-ruby)
variants.implementation_notes: On a GraphQL surface the contract is the Relay connection: first/after (and last/before) slice the field, edges carry an opaque cursor per node, and pageInfo exposes hasNextPage/endCursor so clients can continue; graphql-ruby's GraphQL::Pagination::Connection generates base64 cursors, enforces max_page_size and can expose totalCount. It is the same pattern with the token promoted into the schema: field arguments pin the filter and ordering, and the resolver turns the decoded after cursor into a keyset predicate.
variants.code_sketch:
field :products, ProductType.connection_type, null: false do
  argument :category, String, required: false
end

def products(category: nil)
  scope = Product.order(created_at: :desc, id: :desc)
  category ? scope.where(category: category) : scope
end
# client: products(first: 100, after: endCursor) { edges { cursor node { id } } pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } }
pitfalls: An after cursor produced under different field arguments or a different relation yields an incoherent page unless the resolver pins the arguments (or embeds and re-validates them in the cursor).
Without configuring max_page_size a client can request the entire collection through first, defeating the bounded-page guarantee; totalCount is also expensive on large relations and should be opt-in.
